content: A successful HIV patient monitoring system relies on the collaborative efforts and cooperation of various health sector partners. These include HIV programs, which should establish a standardized minimum dataset as the foundation of any national HIV patient monitoring system. This dataset must define the data collected from any system, whether paper-based or along the paper-to-electronic continuum. Facilities with greater resources may collect additional data. Standardized tools are essential for supervision, data aggregation, and the transfer of clients between facilities and community service delivery sites. The HIV patient monitoring system is a critical component of any national health information system (HIS). Individual data elements should be standardized and well-defined, with data exchange standards established. Similarly, the indicators derived from these data should be clearly defined. Electronic systems should also be harmonized. At a minimum, the HIS should include priority national HIV indicators and adhere to data standards. The patient monitoring system will contribute to many of these indicators. Given the strong links between HIV services and maternal, newborn, and child health (MNCH) and tuberculosis (TB) programs, it is crucial to harmonize relevant data elements across programs. For example, the number of pregnant women receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART) may be reported by both antenatal care (ANC) clinics and HIV clinics. This harmonization is also relevant for other programs, such as sexually transmitted infections (STIs), viral hepatitis, and cervical cancer. With the scale-up of ART, HIV is now among several treatable chronic diseases requiring longitudinal patient follow-up. Collaboration between related national programs, including TB, MNCH, sexual and reproductive health, STIs, other communicable and chronic disease programs, and strategic information units or the HIS, is essential for the success of the HIV program. Recommended activities include using HIV patient cards and ART registers, or their electronic equivalents, at TB and MNCH sites; integrating HIV patient monitoring information into health facility patient folders or patient cards; reconciling program registers to avoid double-counting; integrating service delivery at facilities (e.g., providing ANC and HIV care at the same location for pregnant HIV-positive women); integrating HIV data into other program records and the HIS; standardizing HIV indicators across program areas; and adopting unique identifiers (UIDs) to enable longitudinal tracking of clients across multiple service delivery areas. Patient monitoring requires the participation of a wide range of staff with overlapping responsibilities. Task-shifting to lower-level cadres and lay providers can enhance program capacity. For electronic systems, electronic medical records (EMRs) may replace paper-based patient records, but staff responsibilities remain consistent. Once roles and responsibilities are identified, it is essential to provide necessary training and follow-up to ensure all patient monitoring activities are conducted correctly and efficiently. Strengthening human resources for patient monitoring involves training, clinical mentoring, and supervision. District health management teams and HIS/monitoring and evaluation (M&E) focal points should supervise the monitoring system to ensure quality care and data, discuss data use for improving patient care and service delivery, integrate patient monitoring into clinical mentoring and supervision visits, periodically review the monitoring system, assist staff with data analysis and reporting, provide feedback from previous reports and data quality assurance activities, and offer on-the-spot training to support patient monitoring, data use, and data quality. Health facility in-charges should be familiar with existing patient monitoring tools, ensure adequate training for staff, validate and analyze reports before submission, address patient monitoring during routine visits, maintain strong relationships with district health management teams, provide feedback to staff, and stay updated on changes to the patient monitoring system. Triage workers, receptionists, or data clerks should maintain appointment systems, retrieve patient records, record patient data, generate lists of patients lost to follow-up (LTFU), and support tracing activities. ART aides, lay counselors, or professional counselors should record patient data, support follow-up activities, and identify patients needing clinical visits, drug refills, laboratory tests, or referrals. Nurses, clinical officers, or other clinicians should record patient data in patient records or electronic tools, tally data, complete routine reports, conduct patient reviews with the clinical team, use data to discuss patient management, review program reports to track progress, and assess the quality of HIV services and patient records. Data clerks or administrative staff responsible for data entry, management, and reporting should report on key HIV performance data, organize and manage patient records, transcribe data, enter data into databases or EMRs, tally data, complete routine reports, and review data quality. Community health workers or service providers should initiate HIV testing and ART in the community, monitor adherence and drug pick-up, follow up on LTFU individuals, record patient data in community ART tools or electronic systems, and use data to identify clients needing follow-up or referrals. External clinical mentors and supportive supervisors should review the quality of HIV patient records, provide advice and recommendations to improve clinical care and monitoring, and support data use. Pharmacists and pharmacy technicians/assistants should dispense drugs, manage drug-related toxicity, report adverse drug reactions, provide adherence counseling, and record ARV dispensing in pharmacy records. Facility-based lay providers should enroll patients, provide adherence counseling and treatment education, assess adherence, and track LTFU patients. Training should use patient monitoring data to identify areas of weakness and strength, integrate training into pre-service education, provide ongoing in-service training, support trainees, and ensure staff take refresher courses or continuing education. Clinical mentoring and supportive supervision should involve experienced clinicians providing ongoing training and advice to less experienced providers, helping them develop skills, grow professionally, and improve care quality. Over time, many high-burden HIV countries have transitioned from paper-based systems to electronic information systems, including EMRs. This transition is driven by challenges in retrieving data from paper-based systems, the effort required to maintain such systems as data volume increases, the need for integration across service delivery areas, and increased investments in digital health innovations. However, coverage of electronic systems across all facilities remains suboptimal in many settings, necessitating the continued use of aggregate data systems for reporting. Transitioning to EMRs requires addressing issues such as UIDs, data system interoperability, and data security and confidentiality. Establishing high-quality individual-level data is the first step to improving reporting and data use at all levels.
